params.question: Selective toxicity means an antimicrobial drug can destroy the pathogen with absolutely no risk to the host.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The narration clarified that no drug is perfectly selective; every antimicrobial carries some risk to the host. Selective toxicity aims to widen the therapeutic window between effective and toxic doses by targeting structures unique to the pathogen, not to eliminate host risk entirely.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Paul Ehrlich's 'magic bullet' is an ideal, not reality. As the narration stated, no drug is perfectly selective — every antimicrobial carries some host risk. Selective toxicity means exploiting pathogen-specific targets to maximise the gap between the effective and toxic doses.

interactions.label: A patient on erythromycin develops macrolide resistance. Why would the clinician

params.question: A patient on erythromycin develops macrolide resistance. Why would the clinician expect clindamycin to also be ineffective against the same organism?

answers.text: Both drugs are metabolised by the same hepatic cytochrome P450 enzyme

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Shared hepatic metabolism does not explain microbiological cross-resistance. The reason is that both drugs bind overlapping sites on the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit.

answers.text: Both drugs share overlapping binding sites on the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Macrolides and clindamycin bind overlapping sites on the 50S subunit, so a single ribosomal mutation conferring resistance to one commonly affects the other — a pattern known clinically as MLSB resistance.

answers.text: Both drugs inhibit peptidoglycan cross-linking in the bacterial cell wall

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cell wall synthesis is the target of beta-lactams and glycopeptides, not macrolides or clindamycin. Both erythromycin and clindamycin are 50S ribosomal protein synthesis inhibitors.

answers.text: Both drugs block the same step in the bacterial folate synthesis pathway

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Folate synthesis is inhibited by sulphonamides and trimethoprim, not macrolides or lincosamides. Erythromycin and clindamycin both target the 50S ribosomal subunit.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the five antibacterial target sites. Macrolides (e.g. erythromycin) and clindamycin share overlapping binding sites on the 50S ribosomal subunit, which is why resistance to one often confers resistance to the other.
Well done. Recognising shared binding sites helps predict cross-resistance patterns — a key principle when switching antibiotics after treatment failure.

interactions.label: A patient starting anti-tubercular therapy with HRZE is also on warfarin for a p

params.question: A patient starting anti-tubercular therapy with HRZE is also on warfarin for a prosthetic heart valve. Which property of rifampicin necessitates adjusting the warfarin dose?

answers.text: Rifampicin competes with warfarin for plasma protein binding sites

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Protein binding displacement causes only transient effects. Rifampicin's clinically important interaction is potent induction of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, which accelerates warfarin metabolism.

answers.text: Rifampicin induces hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, accelerating warfarin metabolism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Rifampicin is one of the most potent CYP450 inducers known. It speeds up metabolism of warfarin, oral contraceptives, and many other drugs — making dose adjustment essential during anti-TB therapy.

answers.text: Rifampicin chelates warfarin in the gut, reducing its oral absorption

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Gut chelation is seen with divalent cations (e.g. antacids with tetracyclines), not with rifampicin. The interaction is hepatic enzyme induction accelerating warfarin clearance.

answers.text: Rifampicin directly inactivates warfarin through a chemical reaction in the bloodstream

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no direct chemical inactivation. Rifampicin's interaction with warfarin is indirect — it induces hepatic enzymes that metabolise warfarin faster, reducing its anticoagulant effect.

overallFeedback.feedback: The narration highlighted that rifampicin 'speeds up how the liver breaks down many other medications.' This is because rifampicin potently induces hepatic CYP450 enzymes, requiring dose adjustment of co-administered drugs like warfarin and oral contraceptives.
Exactly right. Remembering rifampicin's potent enzyme induction helps anticipate drug interactions across all HRZE-treated patients.

interactions.label: A patient has been successfully treated with metronidazole for amoebic dysentery

params.question: A patient has been successfully treated with metronidazole for amoebic dysentery and is now symptom-free. Why is a course of diloxanide furoate still required?

answers.text: Metronidazole is only bacteriostatic against amoebae, so a bactericidal drug is needed to complete the cure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Metronidazole is actually amoebicidal — it kills invasive trophozoites by fragmenting their DNA. The issue is that it acts on tissue forms and does not adequately reach cysts persisting in the bowel lumen.

answers.text: Diloxanide furoate eradicates residual intestinal cysts that the tissue amoebicide cannot adequately reach

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Metronidazole clears the invasive tissue infection, but cysts persisting in the bowel lumen can cause relapse. Diloxanide furoate concentrates in the gut to eliminate these residual cysts — completing the tissue-then-luminal sequence.

answers.text: Diloxanide furoate neutralises the hepatotoxic metabolites of metronidazole

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Diloxanide furoate is a luminal amoebicide, not a hepatoprotective agent. Its role is to eliminate residual bowel cysts after the tissue infection has been cleared.

answers.text: Diloxanide furoate provides systemic coverage to prevent relapse of amoebic liver abscess

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Diloxanide furoate is minimally absorbed — it stays in the gut lumen. Its role is specifically to clear residual intestinal cysts, not to provide systemic coverage.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the two-drug sequential strategy: first a tissue amoebicide (metronidazole) clears the invasive disease, then a luminal amoebicide (diloxanide furoate) mops up residual cysts in the bowel to prevent relapse.
Exactly. The tissue-then-luminal sequence is central to amoebiasis management — metronidazole clears the invasion, diloxanide furoate prevents relapse from residual cysts.

interactions.label: Pyrantel and ivermectin both paralyse helminths, but through opposite mechanisms

params.question: Pyrantel and ivermectin both paralyse helminths, but through opposite mechanisms. Which of the following correctly describes this difference?

answers.text: Pyrantel causes flaccid paralysis; ivermectin causes spastic paralysis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: You have reversed them. Pyrantel locks worm muscles into stiff spastic contraction, while ivermectin opens chloride channels causing flaccid (relaxed) paralysis.

answers.text: Pyrantel causes spastic paralysis; ivermectin opens invertebrate chloride channels causing flaccid paralysis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Pyrantel depolarises worm neuromuscular junctions, causing stiff spastic paralysis so peristalsis sweeps the worm out. Ivermectin opens chloride channels found only in invertebrates, causing flaccid paralysis instead.

answers.text: Both cause flaccid paralysis but act on different ion channel families

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The narration specifically contrasted opposite types of paralysis: pyrantel causes spastic paralysis, while ivermectin causes flaccid paralysis.

answers.text: Pyrantel inhibits microtubule assembly; ivermectin blocks acetylcholine receptors

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Microtubule inhibition is the mechanism of albendazole, not pyrantel. Pyrantel causes depolarising spastic paralysis, while ivermectin opens invertebrate chloride channels causing flaccid paralysis.

overallFeedback.feedback: The narration emphasised opposite paralysis types: pyrantel causes spastic (stiff) paralysis via neuromuscular depolarisation, while ivermectin causes flaccid (relaxed) paralysis via invertebrate chloride channels.
Well done. Distinguishing spastic from flaccid paralysis is key to understanding which anthelmintic suits which clinical situation.

params.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with three days of fever, cough, and sore throat. Examination and investigation suggest a viral upper respiratory infection, but she insists on antibiotics. Which of the following is the strongest justification for withholding antibiotic therapy?

answers.text: Young patients rarely develop secondary bacterial complications from viral infections

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Age alone does not determine complication risk. The primary justification is that antibiotics provide no benefit against viruses and their unnecessary use drives antimicrobial resistance in the community.

answers.text: Antibiotics for viral infections provide no clinical benefit and their unnecessary use is a major driver of antimicrobial resistance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The narration identified prescribing for viral infections as one of the biggest drivers of resistance. Step one of rational prescribing is determining whether an antibiotic is needed at all — resisting patient pressure here is itself part of good prescribing.

answers.text: Antibiotics should never be prescribed without a positive culture result

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is too absolute — many bacterial infections are appropriately treated empirically before culture results return. The core issue here is that the infection is viral, making antibiotics ineffective regardless of culture status.

answers.text: Oral antibiotics have poor penetration into upper respiratory tract tissue

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Many oral antibiotics achieve good respiratory tract concentrations. The reason to withhold here is that the illness is viral — antibiotics offer no benefit against viruses and their overuse drives community resistance.

overallFeedback.feedback: The narration's rational prescribing framework begins with: 'Ask whether an antibiotic is even needed.' Prescribing antibiotics for viral infections drives community resistance and provides no patient benefit.
Exactly. Step one of rational prescribing — determining whether an antibiotic is needed at all — is the most powerful intervention against unnecessary resistance.
